subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which economic sector involves the extraction of raw materials from the land or sea?
questions.explain: The primary sector extracts raw materials, for example through farming, fishing, forestry and mining.

questions.q: The manufacturing and processing of raw materials into finished goods belongs to which sector?
questions.explain: The secondary sector turns raw materials into manufactured products, such as in factories and construction.

questions.q: Providing services such as retail, healthcare and tourism is an example of which sector?
questions.explain: The tertiary sector provides services rather than producing goods.

questions.q: Which sector is chiefly concerned with research, information technology and high-tech knowledge-based work?
questions.explain: The quaternary sector involves knowledge-based activities such as research, development and information services.

questions.q: According to the Clark-Fisher model, what generally happens to employment as a country develops economically?
options: Primary employment falls while tertiary employment rises
Primary employment rises while tertiary employment falls
All three sectors stay exactly equal
questions.explain: The Clark-Fisher model shows primary employment declining and tertiary (then quaternary) employment growing as development advances.

questions.q: What does the term deindustrialisation describe?
options: The rapid growth of new factories
An increase in mining and farming jobs
The building of new power stations
questions.explain: Deindustrialisation is the fall in the importance and employment of the secondary (manufacturing) sector.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the informal sector of employment?
options: Unofficial, unregulated work that is not taxed or recorded
Government jobs with fixed salaries and contracts
Regulated employment with pensions and paid leave
questions.explain: Informal-sector work is unofficial and unregulated, such as street trading, and is common in many lower-income cities.

questions.q: A country records 65% of its workforce in the primary sector and only 15% in tertiary. What does this most strongly suggest?
options: It is at a low level of economic development
It is a highly developed post-industrial economy
It has a very large quaternary sector
questions.explain: A large primary workforce with a small tertiary share is typical of a less economically developed, pre-industrial economy.

questions.q: Which group lists only non-renewable fossil fuels?
questions.explain: Coal, oil and natural gas are the three fossil fuels and are all finite, non-renewable resources.

questions.q: Which of the following is a renewable energy source?
questions.explain: Wind is a renewable resource because it is naturally replenished and will not run out.

questions.q: Which fuel is used to generate electricity in a nuclear power station?
questions.explain: Nuclear power stations use uranium as fuel, releasing energy through nuclear fission.

questions.q: Which physical condition is most important for generating hydroelectric power (HEP)?
options: A reliable supply of fast-flowing or dammed water
questions.explain: HEP relies on moving water, so a steady, high-volume water supply and suitable relief for dams are essential.

questions.q: Why do higher-income countries (HICs) generally consume more energy per person than lower-income countries?
options: They have more industry, transport and domestic appliances
They have banned the use of fossil fuels
They rely only on human and animal power
questions.explain: Greater industrialisation, car ownership and use of appliances raise per-capita energy demand in HICs.

questions.q: Iceland generates a large share of its electricity and heating from geothermal energy. Which factor best explains this?
options: It lies on a plate boundary with volcanic activity near the surface
It has very high year-round sunshine
It has extensive tropical rainforest for biomass
It has no access to any water resources
questions.explain: Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, so hot rocks and volcanic activity near the surface make geothermal energy viable.

questions.q: What is meant by a country's 'energy mix'?
options: The range of different energy sources it uses
The total number of power stations it owns
The amount of oil it imports each year
The price households pay for electricity
questions.explain: The energy mix is the combination of energy sources, both renewable and non-renewable, that a country relies on.

questions.q: A country imports almost all of its oil and gas from a single foreign supplier. This situation most clearly reduces its:
questions.explain: Dependence on one foreign supplier makes energy supply vulnerable to disruption, lowering energy security.

questions.q: Sustainable development is best defined as development that:
options: Meets the needs of the present without compromising future generations
Uses up resources as quickly as possible
Ignores environmental impacts to boost profit
questions.explain: This is the widely used Brundtland definition, balancing present needs with the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

questions.q: What does a person's or country's 'carbon footprint' measure?
options: The amount of greenhouse gases produced by their activities
The land area covered by forests
The number of power stations built
The distance travelled by imported goods only
questions.explain: A carbon footprint is the total greenhouse gas emissions caused by an individual, organisation or country.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of energy conservation?
options: Improving home insulation to reduce heating demand
Opening a new coal-fired power station
questions.explain: Conservation reduces energy waste and demand, for example through better insulation and more efficient appliances.

questions.q: A city government wants to make its transport more sustainable. Which measure best fits this aim?
options: Expanding electric public transport and cycle lanes
Subsidising cheaper petrol for private cars
Removing bus routes to cut costs
questions.explain: Promoting low-carbon public transport and cycling cuts emissions and fossil-fuel use, supporting sustainability.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Geography (4GE1) specification; Economic Activity & Energy
